## Biography

I'm a postdoctoral fellow at Gateway Antarctica, University of Canterbury, located in Christchurch, New Zealand. My research focuses on using synthetic aperture radar (SAR), a satellite radar technology that can penetrate through clouds and darkness, to measure changes in glaciers, ice shelves, and sea ice.

I received my PhD in Antarctic Studies from the University of Canterbury in 2023, where my thesis was titled *Ice Tongue Stability in a Changing Climate*. My work was on SAR remote sensing, ice ocean interactions and ice dynamics. Through my published research, I explored how the loss of land-fast sea ice contributed to the collapse of the Parker Ice Tongue, how ocean currents affect the Erebus Ice Tongue, and the interaction between land-fast sea ice and ice shelves.

Prior to my PhD, I completed an MSc in Oceanography at the Universidade Federal do Rio Grande in Brazil in 2018, where I started applying SAR technology to my glacier studies. My academic journey began with a degree in Industrial Engineering from the Pontificia Universidad Católica de Valparaíso in Chile, which I completed in 2006. I also gained over a decade of experience in engineering and tourism, and served as a project manager and researcher at the CEQUA research centre in Chile from 2014 to 2018.

From 2023 to 2026, I served as a Geospatial Research Scientist at the Waterways Centre of the University of Canterbury. During this period, I developed national methods for mapping New Zealand's braided rivers for the Ministry for the Environment. I also led the adaptation of the Riverscapes Framework and its data portal, the [Riverscapes Data Exchange](https://data.riverscapes.net/), to cover New Zealand as a national project. I also worked on various lidar projects and created a test case using ML to estimate forest carbon from airborne lidar for the Ministry for Primary Industries.

Currently, my projects include understanding fast ice growth using SAR data, cal/val of ESA's BIOMASS satellite over Antarctic ice shelves, automatic detection of emperor penguin colonies using high-resolution SAR imagery, as well as using data from the RADARSAT Constellation Mission to monitor end-of-summer snowlines on glaciers in the New Zealand Alps.

## Community

I am currently the chair of the New Zealand chapter of the IEEE Geoscience and Remote Sensing Society (GRSS) and serve on the GRSS IFT working group. I organised the [New Zealand SAR Workshop](teaching.qmd#sar-workshop-2024) (4 September 2024) and the [second New Zealand Radar Remote Sensing School](teaching.qmd#radar-school-2026) (15–17 April 2026). Additionally, I have helped coordinate themes and sessions for IGARSS 2025 and 2026, which is the largest conference in remote sensing. I also co-supervise research students who are working with satellite data.

## Research interests

- Antarctic ice shelves, ice tongues and their interaction with the ocean
- Land-fast sea ice and sea ice
- Ice flow, surface change and mass balance measured from space
- SAR methods: interferometry (InSAR), offset tracking and backscatter analysis
- Combining radar, lidar, multispectral and field data, including machine learning
- Data fusion and machine learning for Earth Observation
